newsitem.title: UK: As oil rallies, grains and metals sink.
newsitem.headline: As oil rallies, grains and metals sink.

text.p: Metals and wheat markets fell sharply on Wednesday and only crude oil kept the recent boom in world raw material prices afloat as it swept to a post-Gulf War high on renewed Iraq tension.

Benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil futures for October hit $23.82 per barrel, up almost $1, after Washington said Iraq fired missiles at U.S. jets over northern Iraq. They missed their targets but the United States also moved B-52 bombers to a base in the Indian Ocean to back its threat of new military strikes on Iraq.
Low stocks of heating fuel ahead of the northern hemisphere winter also support the surge in oil prices.
But elsewhere in commodities, turbulent markets that, not so long ago, raised a spectre of inflation, seemed to be going off the boil.
Aluminium tumbled to its lowest for two years on the London Metal Exchange at $1,437 a tonne as speculative investment funds lost faith in the strength of demand for metals and sold off.

Prices were last at these levels in August 1994 at the start of a blistering rally. Aluminium reached $2,195 in January 1995. "Generally, it is just sentiment...aluminium has led the way down," said analyst Jim Lennon of brokers Macquarie Equities. "Demand simply has not picked up and the longer consumers delay the larger the stock overhang will be," said Angus MacMillan who is an analyst at Billiton Metals said.
Demand prospects are mixed for industrial metals. There is good growth in the U.S. economy but the U.S Federal Reserve likely to cool it with a rate rise before too long.
In the European Union the need to meet convergence criteria for monetary union may slow expansion in 1997.
"We are looking at growth next year of 1.50 percent, which does not translate into great metal demand," MacMillan said.
Also in trouble was palladium, a rare white metal used primarily in electronics and the car industry. It closed on London near a three-year low at $122.25 per ounce, down $1.75 on the day.
Palladium was hit by a wave of selling after easing for several months because of steady Russian metal sales and sluggish Japanese electronics demand.
Sentiment in copper was soured back in June when Sumitomo Corp of Japan fired Yasuo Hamanaka, its star trader and a mastermind behind firm prices, alleging he lost $1.8 billion on maverick trades.
That sounded the death knell for a bull run on copper and it is down from $2,715 in May to just above $1,900 now.
Grain prices fell sharply again on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Wednesday.

Already down from an all-time high in March at $7.50 per bushel, the nearby wheat futures contract gave up on a bid to rally back above $4.60 and eased below $4.50 by mid-session. Latest data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture on Wednesday added to a belief that bigger harvests are easing pressure on world grain stocks.

Stocks had been depleted by 1994 drought in Russia, Australia and North Africa to the lowest in 20 years. "Wheat is dead meat," a trader said. "You added two million tonnes to the Australian crop. The wheat supply is growing. It's going to a buyer's market from a seller's market."
The USDA raised the estimate of the Australian wheat crop to 19.5 million tonnes from 17.5 million previously expected. Also, Imports by China are seen down by 5.0 million tonnes.
